questions.question: Describe Merton's strain theory and evaluate how well it explains crime.

points.text: Merton: society promotes success but restricts legitimate means -> strain -> deviant adaptations. Innovation (theft for success) is the most common criminal response. Strengths: explains why crime is higher in deprived areas; explains white-collar crime (innovation at all class levels). questions.question: Explain how labelling theory accounts for crime and deviance, using Becker's ideas.

points.text: Becker: deviance is created by society's response, not the act itself. Primary deviance (minor, unlabelled) is common. Labelling someone as 'criminal' can cause secondary deviance (they accept the label and act accordingly). The label becomes a master status that overrides other identities. questions.question: Evaluate whether Marxist or Feminist explanations provide a better understanding of crime.

points.text: Marxist: crime is caused by capitalism (exploitation, inequality, greed). Explains both working-class and white-collar crime. Strengths: links crime to economic structure; explains selective enforcement. Weaknesses: not all capitalist societies have high crime; ignores gender; overemphasises class. markScheme.exemplarAnswer: A grade 9 response will: describe Becker's labelling theory (primary/secondary deviance, master status, deviant career); support with Young's hippie study and Cicourel's police discretion; evaluate strengths (explains how deviance escalates, challenges assumptions about criminals, shows power of societal reaction); evaluate weaknesses (doesn't explain primary deviance, implies no crime without labels, overstates the power of labels - some people resist them); conclude: labelling theory provides valuable insights into how social processes CREATE deviance, but it is incomplete - it needs to be combined with structural explanations (Merton, Marxism) that explain why some groups are more likely to be labelled and why primary deviance occurs in the first place.
